text.slice: Firmware Packing
When packing, many options are available — from filesystem type to compression and final file format. Let's go through each one in detail.
Pack Type: ext4 / erofs / f2fs
ext4

A classic journaling filesystem with write support (read-write). Used on partitions that must remain modifiable (userdata, sometimes system on older non-Treble devices). Well-studied, maximally compatible, but takes up more space than erofs with the same content.
erofs

Enhanced Read-Only File System — a compressed read-only filesystem. Used on almost all modern firmware for system/vendor/product and similar partitions that must not be modified at runtime. Due to compression, the final image is noticeably smaller, and reading is faster than from uncompressed ext4.
f2fs

Flash-Friendly File System — a filesystem designed specifically for the characteristics of NAND flash memory (log-structured writes). Typically used for userdata/metadata where write speed and memory wear resistance are important.
Permissions: ro
RO — Read Only. When enabled, the partition cannot be modified directly while the firmware is running on the device (the system will mount it as immutable).
This option only works with ext4 pack type — erofs is always read-only by nature, and f2fs is read-write, so this flag does not apply to them.
Size
Auto
The final file size is determined based on the actual volume of unpacked data — the minimum required size to fit the content.
Original
The final file size will be the same as the original (source) image. If the data turns out to be larger than what fits in the original size, packing will fail with an error.
For kernel, the "Original" mode is always used — this option is fixed for it and unavailable for selection.
img Format: raw / sparse
raw
A full sector-by-sector partition image — a universal format understood by any tool (dd, image analyzers, etc.), but takes up more disk space on the phone during the packing stage.
sparse

Android sparse format — stores only actually occupied blocks, empty areas are not written. Smaller in size and what fastboot expects when flashing via "fastboot flash". Cannot be read directly by third-party tools without conversion (img2simg/simg2img).
What to choose:
If you plan to flash via fastboot — choose sparse. If you need an image for analysis/unpacking/dd — raw.
This option is only available with ext4/erofs pack type — f2fs does not support this setting.
File Format: img / .dat / .dat.br
img
A regular partition image (raw or sparse) — for flashing via fastboot or dd directly.
.dat
A block-based data transfer format (transfer list) used by update_engine/recovery when installing via updater-script — used on non-A/B systems without dynamic partitions.
.dat.br
Same as .dat, but additionally compressed with brotli — reduces file size, often used in OTA/updater packages for non-A/B firmware.
br (brotli) Compression Level
7 brotli compression levels are available — from 1 (minimal compression, fastest packing) to 7 (maximum compression, but noticeably longer packing time).

The higher the level, the smaller the final .dat.br file, but the longer the packing itself takes. For everyday repacking, medium values are sufficient; the maximum level should be used when minimal file size is critical (e.g., for distribution).
Firmware Compression Level (erofs/f2fs)

9 levels — from 1 (minimal compression, fastest packing and unpacking on the device) to 9 (maximum compression, minimal partition size, but higher CPU load on the device when reading and longer packing itself).
A higher level is useful when device storage space is critical. For a balance of speed/size, a medium level is usually sufficient.
Compression Type (erofs)
lz4
The fastest decompression on the device, but also the lowest compression ratio — minimal CPU load when reading.
lz4hc
"High Compression" version of lz4 — compresses noticeably better than regular lz4 (packing itself takes longer), but decompression speed on the device remains almost as fast as lz4.
lzma

The maximum compression ratio of all three, but the slowest decompression — higher CPU load on the device every time files are read from the partition. Should only be used if size is more important than performance.
Compress ext4 Space
Shrinks the ext4 filesystem to the minimum required size, removing empty reserved space — the final file becomes more compact, without unnecessary "air" inside the image.
Only works for ext4 — for erofs, the final size is already calculated based on the actual packed data, and f2fs does not support this operation.
Remove AVB Data Encryption
Removes AVB (Android Verified Boot) flags from fstab and switches the corresponding entries to decrypt mode.

In practice, this means: the userdata partition no longer requires forced encryption (forceencrypt/fileencryption), and the system no longer checks partition integrity via AVB signatures when mounting. This is necessary when you manually modify partitions — without disabling AVB, the device may enter a bootloop, since checksums after modification no longer match the expected ones.
Packing super.img
A separate packing of the dynamic super partition, which combines logical partitions (system, vendor, product, etc.)
Super Type
a_only
For single-slot devices (without A/B updates) — only one active set of logical partitions.
ab
For A/B devices (seamless update) — a single super stores two complete sets of partitions with _a/_b suffixes, allowing the inactive slot to be updated without touching the active one.
virtual_ab

A newer scheme (starting from Android 11) — instead of full partition duplication, copy-on-write snapshots are used, saving device storage space during OTA updates. Requires virtual A/B support from the device's fastbootd/bootloader.
Pack Format: raw / sparse

The same principle as with regular img: raw — a full sector-by-sector image, sparse — a compact format that fastboot expects when "fastboot flash super". For flashing via fastboot, sparse is almost always needed.
Total Size

The final size of the entire super.img in gigabytes — must match the actual size of the super partition on the target device (can be checked in the original firmware or via lpdump on the source super.img).
Group Name
Default: qti_dynamic_partitions

This is the partition group name used by lpmake when building super — it must match what was in the device's original firmware, otherwise fastbootd/bootloader may not recognize the partition when flashing.

The prefix "qti" (Qualcomm Technologies Inc) means this is the standard name for devices on Qualcomm chipsets — this is historically how most Snapdragon device manufacturers name the group. On devices with other chipsets (MediaTek, Google Tensor, etc.), the group name may differ.

The exact group name for a specific device is best checked in the metadata of the original super.img (e.g., via lpdump) — if you have a non-standard chipset/vendor, there will most likely be a different name, and it must be specified exactly as it was in the original.
